::: {.tldr}
An unsupervised model of evolution that predicts which human variants cause disease, as well as methods trained on clinical labels.
:::

{{< paper-links >}}

**Authors:** Jonathan Frazer, Pascal Notin, Mafalda Dias, Aidan Gomez, Joseph K. Min, Kelly Brock, Yarin Gal & Debora S. Marks

## In plain language

Genetic testing finds many variants in patients that nobody has seen before. For most of them, doctors cannot say whether they cause disease. Labelling them one by one, through clinical evidence or experiments, cannot keep pace with the number of possible variants.

EVE takes a different route. For each human protein, it learns from the matching proteins in a huge range of other species which amino acids are tolerated at each position over evolutionary time. Changes that evolution has never allowed are likely to break the protein. The model is a Bayesian variational autoencoder, a deep generative model, and it never sees a clinical label.

Despite that, EVE classified known disease variants as accurately as methods trained on clinical labels, and its predictions agreed well with high-throughput experiments. We used it to score tens of millions of variants across thousands of disease-associated genes, giving evidence for many variants that were previously of uncertain significance. EVE is the foundation for later models from the group, including popEVE.

## Key figure

::: {.key-figure}
![**Figure 1.** EVE overview. For each protein, a Bayesian variational autoencoder learns the distribution of sequences across evolution; the log-likelihood ratio of mutant to wild type gives an evolutionary index, and a Gaussian mixture model turns it into a pathogenicity score that can be combined with other clinical evidence. From the preprint, Frazer et al., bioRxiv (2020), [CC BY-NC-ND 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).](figure1.png)
:::
